title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Three Groups


What your backtest earned, and what you compared it against
What changed when you switched to ARY and datekey
The thing that broke



If your annual return went down when you fixed the point-in-time problem, that is the most useful slide anyone will show today. Say by how much.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
What the Peer Median Assumes

That every company in an industry deserves the same multiple.


Two software companies, same industry. One grows at twenty percent with a forty percent margin; the other grows at three percent and barely breaks even. The peer median says they should trade at the same P/E, and calls the difference mispricing.

It is not mispricing. It is the model being wrong.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
The Alternative


Borrow a multiple
Find companies that look like this one. Use the middle of what they trade at.


Predict a multiple
Estimate what the market pays for growth, for profitability, for leverage. Apply those prices to this company.



The second one is a regression, and the first one is a special case of it — a regression on industry dummies and nothing else.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Freeze a Date

One row per company, on a single day. Three thousand rows, and no time dimension at all.

Tell GLM

Build a cross-section as of June 30 of last year: one row per stock, with P/E from daily, and from the most recent sf1 annual filing bring in ROE, revenue growth, the operating margin, leverage, and payout. Add sector.


Everything today happens inside this one table. The time series comes back at the end.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
What Goes on the Left


P/E
Bounded below at zero, unbounded above, and violently skewed. OLS on this is mostly fitting the tail.


log P/E
Roughly symmetric. Coefficients read as percentage effects on the multiple, which is how you want to think about them anyway.



And the negative-earnings problem does not go away — you cannot take the log of a negative P/E, so those companies leave the sample. Note how many, and which kind.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
What Goes on the Right







Growth
Revenue growth, earnings growth — what the multiple is supposed to be paying for


Profitability
ROE, ROA, margins


Risk
Leverage, and how variable the earnings have been


Size
Log market cap


Sector
Dummies — which is where the peer median hides




Start with a handful you can defend. A regression with forty right-hand variables is a machine learning problem, and that is Tuesday.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Run It
Tell GLM

Regress log P/E on those characteristics with sector fixed effects. Winsorize the right-hand variables at 1 and 99 percent. Show me the coefficients, the standard errors, and the R-squared.


Then read the coefficients before you look at anything else. Does the market pay more for growth? For profitability? If a sign is backwards, that is the finding, and it usually means a variable is built wrong.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
What R-Squared to Expect

Somewhere between a third and a half. Which is enormous, and does not mean what you want it to mean.


Cross-sectional valuation regressions fit well because companies genuinely do trade on their fundamentals. The question is not whether the fit is good. It is whether what is left over is worth trading.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Fitted and Residual


Fitted
What the market, on average, pays for a company with these characteristics.


Actual
What this company actually trades at.


Residual
The gap. Negative means it trades below what its own characteristics justify.



The residual is the signal, and it is exactly the same shape as last session’s signal — own multiple against a predicted one. All that changed is how the prediction is made.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
section: Two Readings of a Negative Residual
text:
Two Readings of a Negative Residual


It is cheap
The market has not noticed. Buy it, wait for the gap to close.
This is the assumption the whole strategy rests on.

Your model is missing something
The company is in litigation, or its growth is about to stop, and the market knows. The gap is information you failed to include.


You cannot tell these apart for any single company. You can only find out in aggregate, over many companies and many years, which is what the backtest is for.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Look at the Extremes
Tell GLM

Show me the twenty largest positive and twenty largest negative residuals, with their characteristics and their sector.


If the cheap list is all one sector, your sector dummies are not doing their job. If it is all microcaps, size is entering the pricing in a way your model has not captured. Either way you learn it in thirty seconds by looking.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Against Last Session

The peer median is the same regression with only sector dummies on the right.

Tell GLM

Fit it three ways on this cross-section: sector dummies only, characteristics only, and both. Compare the R-squared and the correlation between the three sets of residuals.


If the residuals correlate at 0.9, the extra machinery is not buying you a new signal. It is buying you the same signal with more steps.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Refit Every Year

One regression per year, using only that year’s data.


The temptation is to fit once on everything and apply the coefficients throughout. That uses 2024 data to price a 2004 company. It is the same look-ahead as MRY, wearing a different hat, and it is harder to spot because nothing about the code looks wrong.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
The Loop


For each June 30 from 2001 to 2025, build the cross-section
Fit the regression on that year alone
Take the residuals
Sort into deciles, long the cheapest, short the most expensive
Hold twelve months, record the return



Step 2 is the only thing that changed from Tuesday. Everything else is the backtest you already have — which is the point of having written it as code you can read.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Watch the Coefficients Move
Tell GLM

Plot each coefficient by year, with its confidence band.


The price of growth is not a constant. If a coefficient flips sign in 2009 and again in 2021, that is worth a slide in your presentation — and it is a reason to be suspicious of any model that assumes the relationship is fixed.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
section: How Many Companies Survive Each Year
text:
How Many Companies Survive Each Year
Tell GLM

For each year, report how many stocks had all the variables and how many were dropped, broken out by which variable was missing.


Every characteristic you add shrinks the sample, and it does not shrink it randomly. A model that requires five years of earnings history is a model estimated on established companies only.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Three Backtests, One Table



Peer median
Tuesday’s result


Regression residual
Today’s


Plain P/E
No prediction at all — just buy the low multiples




Report the average annual return, the volatility, the t-stat, and the worst year for all three. Same dates, same universe, same weighting, or the comparison means nothing.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
The Honest Outcome

It is entirely possible that plain P/E wins.


That would be a real result, and a well-known one. The elaborate model has more ways to be wrong, more parameters to fit to noise, and a smaller sample to fit them on. Report it if you find it.

What you must not do is keep trying specifications until one of them beats the others, and then present that one.

title: Linear Regression for Multiples
text:
Three Things


Get the annual refit loop running, and produce the three-way comparison table
Save the cross-section builder as a skill — you will use it every week from here
Write the memory file, including which specifications you tried and rejected



Tuesday we replace the regression with something that can find relationships you did not specify. Come with the linear result written down, because it is the benchmark that machine learning has to beat.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Three Things


The data — twenty-five years of fundamentals and prices, and how to reach it
Skills — how you stop re-explaining yourself to the machine
Build one — a valuation skill that prices a company off its peers



By the end you will have something in your group’s repository that any of you can point at a ticker.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
section: The Oldest Valuation Method There Is
text:
The Oldest Valuation Method There Is

A company is worth roughly what companies like it are worth.


No forecast, no discount rate, no terminal value. Find the peers, take the middle of their multiples, apply it. It is what a banker does on the back of an envelope, and it is a real benchmark — hard to beat and easy to check.

The whole method is three decisions: which multiple, which peers, and what to do with the ones that do not make sense.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
The Rice Business Data Portal


What is in it
Every NYSE and Nasdaq listed common stock, beginning in 2000.


Where it comes from
Licensed by Rice Business from Nasdaq Data Link.


What it is
A DuckDB database. Queries are read-only — SELECT and nothing else.


data-portal.rice-business.org

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Get Your Token


Register at the portal with your rice.edu address
You are issued an access token, good for six months
Put it where the lab can find it — not in a file you commit



The token is yours. A token in a public repository is a token somebody else is using by Thursday.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Three Doors Into It


The web interface
A query window with an AI assistant that writes the SQL for you. Good for looking around.


The Python client
A library for notebooks and scripts. This is what your analysis will use.


The MCP server
GLM queries the database directly, without you writing anything.



The third one is how we will work today. It is also the one that makes it easy to stop paying attention — so we will keep looking at the SQL.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
What Is in There



Table
Contents




sep
Daily open, high, low, close, adjusted close, volume


daily
Daily valuation ratios and market cap


metrics
Daily moving averages and other statistics


sf1
10-K and 10-Q data, and pre-computed financial ratios


sf2
Insider trades, from Form 4


tickers
Industry, sector, exchange, size category


actions
Mergers, splits, dividends, ticker changes


events
SEC 8-K filings and material corporate events




A Table Descriptions page on the portal lists every variable in every table.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
section: Today We Need Three of Them
text:
Today We Need Three of Them


daily
pe, pb, ps, ev, evebit, evebitda, marketcap — one row per stock per day.


tickers
sector, industry, exchange, scalemarketcap. This is what makes a peer group a peer group.


sf1
The filings. Revenue, earnings, book value, and the ratios computed from them.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
sf1 Has Dimensions




Annual
Quarterly
Trailing four quarters




As most recently restated
MRY
MRQ
MRT


As originally reported
ARY
ARQ
ART




Today we use MRY — annual, most recent restatement. It is the cleanest view of what a company earned. When we start backtesting, we will have to switch, because MRY tells you today what nobody knew at the time.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Three Things That Trip Everyone







Dates are text
Cast before you compare or sort: date::DATE, reportperiod::DATE


sf1 has no date
Use reportperiod for the fiscal period end, datekey for the filing date


Market cap is in thousands
In daily. A $2T company shows up as 2,000,000,000




Each of these produces an answer, not an error. That is what makes them expensive.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Start by Looking Around
Tell GLM

Using the data portal, show me the columns in daily and tickers, and give me five rows of each.


Before any analysis, look at the actual rows. Half of the mistakes in this course get caught here, in thirty seconds, by someone who looked.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
The Pull
Tell GLM

For the most recent date in daily, get ticker, pe, and marketcap for every stock. Join sector and industry from tickers. Then pull the MRY rows from sf1 for the most recent fiscal year and bring in revenue, net income, and shares outstanding. Show me the SQL before you run it.


That last sentence is the entire lesson from Tuesday, in six words.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Read the SQL

You are not checking whether it is elegant. You are checking four things.








Did it filter the dimension?
Without dimension = 'MRY' you get six rows per company-year


Did it cast the dates?
Text comparison on dates goes wrong quietly


Is the join key right?
ticker is not unique across time — see actions


How many rows came back?
You know roughly how many listed stocks there are

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
What a P/E of –12 Means

Nothing. It means the company lost money.


A negative P/E is not a cheap stock. It is a stock with no E. Left in the sample it drags the median in the wrong direction and makes the cheapest-looking companies the ones that are losing the most.

Tell GLM

Drop the negative P/E rows, and show me how many you dropped by sector.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Look Before You Compute
Tell GLM

Histogram of P/E across all stocks. Then the same by sector, and a table of the count, median, and the 10th and 90th percentiles in each.


You are looking for two things: how fat the right tail is, and whether the sectors actually differ. If they do not, the peer group is doing no work and the method has nothing to offer.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Why the Median


The mean
One company with a P/E of 900 — a real company that barely broke even — and the average for the industry is meaningless.

The median
Unmoved by the tail. With ratios, where the numerator is bounded below and the denominator can approach zero, this is not a refinement. It is the difference between a number and noise.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Which Peers?


Sector
Eleven of them. Always enough companies, often not comparable ones.


Industry
Much finer. Sometimes four companies, and then the median is one company’s P/E.


Industry and size
Better in principle. Cuts the group again, so you need to watch the count.



There is no correct answer. There is a choice you make, write down, and defend when you present.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
The Calculation


Group the stocks by peer set, and drop the ones with no meaningful P/E
Take the median P/E in each group
Multiply it by the company’s own earnings per share
Compare with the price it actually trades at



The gap is the whole output. A company trading well below its peer median is either cheap or different, and the method cannot tell you which.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Now Do It
Tell GLM

Compute the median P/E within each industry. For every stock, report its own P/E, its industry median, and the ratio of the two. Show me the twenty most expensive and the twenty cheapest by that ratio.


Read the two lists. If the cheap list is all one industry, or all tiny companies, something in the peer definition is doing work you did not intend.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Stop Re-Explaining Yourself


Always on
Applies to every conversation you have.
Who you are, how you want to be written to, what never to do.


Per project
Applies inside one folder.
This course, this dataset, its quirks.


When relevant
A skill: read only when what you asked matches what it is for.



Three scopes, and the third is the interesting one — because it costs nothing until it applies.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
section: A Skill Is Written Instructions, Filed Where They Can Be Found
text:
A Skill Is Written Instructions, Filed Where They Can Be Found
A folder with a SKILL.md in it. Two parts: a line saying when to use it, and the instructions for how.


At startup
It reads only the name and the one-line description — a few dozen words per skill.


When it matches
Only then does it open the file and read the rest.


Which is why you can have many
A hundred installed skills cost nothing until one of them is relevant.



Not a plugin, and not code. A written procedure.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
CLAUDE.md Versus a Skill


CLAUDE.md — always read
What is always true here: what the project is, where things live, the conventions, what never to do.
Read at the start of every session in that folder.

A skill — read when relevant
A procedure for a particular kind of job.
Standing facts go in CLAUDE.md. Procedures go in skills.


Ask GLM to write the first CLAUDE.md for you — it will read the folder and draft it.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
section: Why This Matters to a Group
text:
Why This Matters to a Group

The skill is a file. The file is in the repository.


Which means the decision is made once, by one of you, and the other two get it by pulling. It also means the decision is visible: when you present, the skill is the record of what you chose and why.

Every ad-hoc instruction typed into a prompt window dies with that conversation.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
section: Get It Right Once, Then Save It
text:
Get It Right Once, Then Save It


Get the peer-median valuation working the way you want it, in a conversation
Say: save that as a skill
Start a fresh session and ask it to value a different company



Step 3 is the test. If it needs to be told anything you already decided, the skill is not finished.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
section: What Has to Be Written Down
text:
What Has to Be Written Down


The decisions
Which multiple. Which peer definition. Median, not mean. What the minimum group size is.


The traps
dimension = 'MRY'. Cast the dates. Market cap is in thousands. Drop negative earnings.


The output
What it should hand back every time: the peer set and its size, the median, the implied value, the gap.



The middle card is the one that pays for itself. Those four traps will otherwise bite each of you, separately, for six weeks.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Exercise


Build the skill in your group’s repository
Test it on a company none of you used while building it
Then test it on a bank, and on a company that lost money last year
Commit and push it



Steps 2 and 3 are where you find out what you left implicit. Write down what broke — it is what you will present on Tuesday.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Where It Will Fail


The industry of one
A peer group with three companies in it has a median that is one company’s opinion.


Financials
P/E means something different for a bank. So does book value.


Growth
Two companies in the same industry with different growth rates should not trade at the same multiple. The method assumes they do.



The third one is what Thursday of next week is about: predicting the multiple instead of borrowing it.

title: Median of Peer Multiples
text:
Three Things


Finish the skill, and push it
Run it on five companies you know something about, and see whether the answers are sane
Bring the one case where it was most obviously wrong



Tuesday we turn this into a trade: rank every stock by the gap, buy the cheap ones, sell the expensive ones, and find out what that would have earned.

title: Getting Started
text:
Two Halves


The tool
Generative AI as it is actually used at work: to write and run code.
You will not write Python. You will direct it, and check it.

The subject
Quantitative investing. Predicting stock returns, and finding out how little is predictable.
The data is real, and so are the models.

title: Getting Started
section: What the Model Is Actually Good For
text:
What the Model Is Actually Good For

One claim, and we spend six weeks testing it.


A language model’s comparative advantage is turning text into a number. Everything downstream — sizing, portfolio construction, execution — is an optimization problem the model does not help with.

The corollary is the useful part: it is not going to trade for you, but it will write every line of the machinery that does.

Weeks

6

Expect the model to explain about one percent of the variance. That is not a bug, and we will spend a full session on why it is a good outcome.

title: Getting Started
text:
Andrej Karpathy
OpenAI co-founder, former Tesla AI chief, now at Anthropic


October 2025
“They just don’t work. They don’t have enough intelligence … You can’t just tell them something and they’ll remember it.”

title: Getting Started
text:
Which Means

The same person, three times in four months.


The version of this you formed an opinion about is probably not the version that exists. Almost everything useful arrived in the last eighteen months, and a good deal of it since last December.

title: Getting Started
text:
That Is the Whole Trick

Almost everything useful the model does, it does by writing code and running it.


Usually Python or JavaScript. The code runs on a server — here, on the lab machine — not inside the model.

You are not asking it for an answer. You are asking it for a program that produces an answer, and the program is something you can read.

title: Getting Started
text:
One Capability, Six Directions



Excel workbooks with live formulas
Charts and figures


PowerPoint decks
Data analysis and statistics


Word documents
Web apps and dashboards




These are not six features somebody built. They are one capability — write code, run it — pointed in six directions.

title: Getting Started
text:
What That Looks Like Underneath
You ask

Read these four PDFs. Pull out every number either side cites about market share, note which ones disagree, and put it in a table.

What actually happens
Each PDF is converted to text. The text is read. A Python script builds the table. The table is written to a file.

Nothing there is a document feature. It is code execution, pointed at file formats.

title: Getting Started
text:
Numbers Need Code


The problem
To a next-token predictor, “47.3%” is exactly as plausible as “52.1%”.
Mental math, rankings, comparisons, aggregations — all unreliable, and the wrong number arrives with complete confidence.

The fix
Insist on code, and insist that it run.
Arithmetic stops being prediction and becomes computation — and you can read afterward what it actually did.

title: Getting Started
text:
First, a Chatbot

You, a program, and a model. The model reads text and writes text. That is the entire capability.


It cannot open a file, run a calculation, look up today’s date, or check whether what it just told you is true.

The chatbot passes along your prompt — plus the system prompt and everything said so far in the conversation — and hands back the reply.

title: Getting Started
section: An Agent Is a Chatbot with Tools
text:
An Agent Is a Chatbot with Tools


The agent sends the prompt, the history, and a list of tools it has
The model answers: use tool X, with these arguments
The agent runs tool X and reports the result back, with instructions for reading it
The model decides what to do next — another tool, or an answer for you



The model never runs anything. It emits requests; the agent executes them. Those step-3 instructions are the tool harness, and some are far better than others.

title: Getting Started

What runs
Claude Code, running GLM-4.7.


What is installed
Python, JavaScript, the analysis libraries, and a set of Claude Code plugins.


What you see
A file browser, a terminal, and a browser view for anything you build.



All of it runs in the cloud and is billed to the school.

text:
Two Places Your Group Lives


A GitHub repository
One shared copy of the code, the notebooks, and the results. It is what you show when you present.


A Slack channel
For coordinating between classes. Add me to it.



Set both up this week, and send me the repository URL.

title: Getting Started
text:
Why GitHub

Your group shares one repository, not a folder of attachments.


Mailing notebooks around breaks down by the second week. GitHub keeps one copy that everyone edits, records who changed what and when, and lets two of you work the same afternoon without overwriting each other.

title: Getting Started
section: You Do Not Type Git Commands
text:
You Do Not Type Git Commands

Same bargain as the code. You say what you want; GLM runs it.


Git has a deserved reputation for cryptic errors. You do not need to learn it — you need to know what you are asking for, and to check that it happened.

There is exactly one step you do yourself, and it is on the next slide.

title: Getting Started
text:
Once, Per Person
The one thing GLM cannot do for you


Create a free account at github.com, and note your username
Open the Terminal tab — not the GLM pane
Run gh auth login, and answer: GitHub.com, then HTTPS, then yes to authenticating Git, then log in with a browser
It prints a code — open the link on your laptop and paste it there



The yes in step 3 is the one people miss. Say no and everything looks fine until your first push, which fails asking for a password that no longer exists.

title: Getting Started
text:
One Person Creates the Repo
Tell GLM

Make my workspace a git repository, commit everything in it, and create a private GitHub repo called mgmt638-team1 from it. Then push.


One person in the group does this, once. Everyone else skips to the slide after next.

title: Getting Started
text:
Then Add Your Groupmates
On github.com, in the new repository


Settings, then Collaborators, then Add people
Search each groupmate by their GitHub username
They get an email invitation, and have to accept it



Until someone accepts, their clone fails with “not found” rather than “no permission” — the repository is private, so to them it does not exist yet.

title: Getting Started
text:
Everyone Else Joins
Tell GLM

Clone the GitHub repo alice/mgmt638-team1 into my workspace.


alice is the GitHub username of whoever created the repo, not yours. You should end up with a mgmt638-team1 folder in your workspace — ask GLM to work inside it from now on.

title: Getting Started
text:
Push and Pull
Tell GLM, at the start and end of every session

Pull the latest from GitHub before we start.


Commit what we did with a sensible message and push it.


Pull first, push last. Nearly every tangle you will hit this term comes from skipping one of the two.

title: Getting Started
text:
Good Enough Prompting

Most of the prompt engineering advice from a few years ago is now either useless or actively harmful.



Say what you want, not how to do it
“I want to compare revenue across countries — how should we show it?”
beats
“Make a bar chart, sorted descending, gridlines off, 12pt labels.”


If it does not work, try again
Rephrasing is cheap. Treat it as an infinitely patient colleague with a poor memory.

title: Getting Started
text:
Plan Before You Act
Use plan mode, or just add: plan how you will do this before you start.


Why it works — knowledge
Planning pulls the relevant considerations into the conversation. It then answers in light of what it just retrieved, rather than from base rates.

Why it works — scale
It breaks the work into steps you can check one at a time. Failures stay small and local instead of surfacing at the very end.

title: Getting Started
text:
Confirm It Understood

Ambiguity does not produce a question. It produces a confident answer to a question you did not ask.

Tell GLM, before it starts

Tell me what you are about to do and what you are assuming.


Correct it in one sentence, then say go ahead. This is the cheapest habit in the course and it will save you the most time.

title: Getting Started
section: It Is a Prediction Machine, Not a Colleague
text:
It Is a Prediction Machine, Not a Colleague
Suppose it told you last week that method A beats method B. Today you ask it to do the task.


What it will do
If “A beats B” is not in this conversation, and B appeared more often in its training data, it will probably use B.

Why
Knowledge in the weights is not knowledge in use. Something has to pull it into the conversation before it can act on it.

title: Getting Started
text:
Tunnel Vision

Prediction also means momentum. Once it has started down a path, continuing that path is the likeliest next step.

You will watch it hit a roadblock, find a way around, hit another, find another way around — tenaciously, exhaustively. What it rarely does is go back and ask whether a different path was better all along.

Restate the goal, not the obstacle. That gives it permission to abandon the path instead of defending it.

title: Getting Started
text:
What Not to Do







Skip
Why




“Think step by step”
Reasoning models already do, in hidden tokens


“Take a deep breath”
Measurably useless now


“CRITICAL! NEVER EVER …”
Overtriggers, and gets worse results


Stacked personas
“You are an expert X” can help tone; three of them does not




Direct task framing wins. Say what you want, say what done looks like, say what to avoid.

title: Getting Started
text:
Go and Get the Data

No file to upload, no API key to paste. Ask.

Tell GLM

Get monthly returns for WMT and SPY since 2020 from Yahoo Finance. Scatter plot, SPY on the horizontal axis, with a regression line.

title: Getting Started
text:
What You Just Did
The slope of that line is Walmart’s market beta. You estimated a CAPM regression by asking for a scatter plot.

The code ran on a machine in the cloud. Nobody at Yahoo, and nobody at Anthropic, built a beta calculator.

title: Getting Started
text:
Look at the Code
Tell GLM

Show me the code you ran.

You do not need to write Python to read it. Find the line that computes the returns.

Any number that matters comes out of code you can open. That rule applies to every session in this course.

title: Getting Started
text:
Push It Further
Tell GLM

Add the other Dow components and rank them by beta.


Annotate the three months with the largest residuals and tell me what happened in each.


Watch whether those explanations are sourced or invented.

title: Getting Started
text:
Put It Somewhere
Tell GLM

Put the chart and a short written summary in a PowerPoint deck.

Then download it and open it on your laptop.

The chart, the layout, the text — all produced by code GLM wrote and ran.

title: Getting Started
text:
What Could Go Wrong

You asked for a chart of betas and you got one. Now what?



No answer
Easy. You notice immediately.


Wrong kind of answer
Also easy. A pie chart when you wanted a scatter.


Right kind, wrong numbers
This is the one. It looks exactly like the answer you wanted.

title: Getting Started
text:
The Trap
Yahoo gives you two closing prices for every day: Close, and Adj Close, which is adjusted for dividends and splits.
Returns from the wrong one are wrong — and Walmart both pays a dividend and split three-for-one in 2024.
Tell GLM

Recompute the betas both ways and show me the difference.

title: Getting Started
text:
Where the Errors Come From


Misunderstanding
Your instruction was ambiguous.
Ask it to state its plan before it starts.


Silent assumptions
It chose something you never authorized — which price column, which date range.
Ask it to walk through what it did.


Coding errors
Rare. The code either runs or it does not.

title: Getting Started
text:
Hallucinations

It is not lying. It is predicting the next token, and a plausible citation is exactly as predictable as a real one.


The risk is highest when the answer is unknown or unfindable — an obscure statistic, a citation that may not exist, a number that was never public. Asked a question with no available answer, it will still produce one.



Make it search
And give you the sources.


Check the sources
Click them. A real-looking citation to a paper that does not exist is the classic failure.


Make it compute
Any number that matters comes out of code.

title: Getting Started
text:
Never Ask “Is This Good?”

Training on human feedback teaches that agreement earns high ratings. Ask “is my plan sound?” and it will find reasons that it is.

Invert the question

What is the strongest argument that this recommendation is wrong?


One step further: have it play a specific skeptic — a referee, a regulator, the desk that has to trade this.

title: Getting Started
text:
Set a Critic on It

GLM can dispatch a subagent: a fresh instance, no memory of this conversation.



Why it is worth something
It sees the instructions, not the reasoning behind the first answer. It has nothing to defend.
Give it a mandate: find every factual error, logical gap, and unsupported assumption. Do not summarize — find flaws.

The catch
Two agreeing runs are evidence, not proof. They share a model and they share your ambiguous question.


Anything that both produces work and checks its own work is grading its own homework.

title: Getting Started
section: Three Checks Before You Trust It
text:
Three Checks Before You Trust It


Where did this come from?
A citation you can click, a file you can open, or code you can read. If none of the three, treat it as a guess.


What did it assume?
Every unstated choice was made for you. Ask what it decided that you did not specify.


Would I catch it if it were wrong?
If not, that is the part to check by hand — not the part you already understand.

title: Getting Started
text:
AQR Capital Management


1998 founded, out of Chicago and Goldman


$189B under management


No. 1 largest hedge fund manager, 2025


A firm whose entire investment process is an argument published in journals.
Background: AQR Capital Management

title: Getting Started
text:
Quality Minus Junk

Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen, “Quality minus junk”, Review of Accounting Studies, 2019.

Watch the video

Quality is one of the characteristics you will put in your own model in week three. This is where it comes from.

title: Getting Started
text:
Four Things


Settle your group — two or three people
Set up the group’s GitHub repository and Slack channel, and send me both
Read the AQR background note
Bring a question about something GLM got wrong today



Thursday we start on valuation: what a company is worth compared with the companies it looks like.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Starting Today


Three groups, drawn at random, at the start of every class
Five minutes each, on what you got done last session
Show the repository — the skill, the code, the numbers



What broke is more interesting than what worked, and it is what the rest of the room needs to hear. A presentation that reports only success is a presentation nobody learns from.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
What to Cover


What you decided
Which multiple, which peer group, what minimum size. And why.


What surprised you
The company where the answer was obviously wrong, and what it turned out to be.


What you would change
You have run it now. What is the first thing you would do differently?

title: Trading on Predictions
section: You Have a Number for Every Stock
text:
You Have a Number for Every Stock

Own P/E divided by peer median P/E. Below one is cheap relative to its peers; above one is expensive.


That is a prediction, whether or not you meant it as one. It says: this company should trade closer to its peers than it does.

The question today is whether that prediction is worth anything.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Sort, Do Not Threshold


A threshold
“Buy anything below 0.7.” How many stocks is that? Some years, none. Some years, four hundred.


A sort
“Buy the cheapest tenth.” Always the same number of positions, whatever the market is doing.



Ranking also throws away the scale of the signal, which is the part you trust least. You are betting on the order, not the magnitude.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Long, Short, or Both


Long only
Buy the cheapest decile. Most of what you earn is just the market.


Long-short
Cheapest decile long, most expensive short. What is left is the signal.


Long-short, dollar neutral
Equal dollars each side. The version we will build.



The long-short version is a much harder test, and it is the one that tells you whether you found anything.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
The Loop


Pick a date — the last trading day of June, say
Compute the signal for every stock, using only what was known that day
Sort, and form the portfolio
Hold it for one year. No trading, no rebalancing
Record the return
Move forward a year and do it again



Twenty-odd repetitions. That is your entire sample, and it is worth remembering how small a number that is.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Why Once a Year


The signal moves slowly
It is built from annual filings. Recomputing it monthly gives you eleven months of the same answer and eleven months of trading costs.

And it keeps the test honest
Annual holding periods make the overlapping-returns problem go away. Monthly rebalancing with annual data does not give you twelve times the evidence.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Equal or Value Weighted


Equal weighted
Same dollars in each name. Simple, and dominated by small companies — which is where most anomalies live, and where they are hardest to trade.


Value weighted
Weights by market cap. A much more honest test, and usually a much weaker result.



Report both. A strategy that works equal-weighted and dies value-weighted has told you exactly what it is.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Build It
Tell GLM

Write a backtest. For each year from 2001 to 2025: on June 30, compute the peer-median signal for every stock using the valuation skill, sort into deciles, go long the cheapest decile and short the most expensive, equal weighted, hold twelve months, and record the return. Plan it before you start.


Then read the plan before you let it write anything.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
The Restatement Problem

MRY is the most recent restatement. It tells you today what nobody knew then.


A company that restated its 2008 earnings in 2011 shows up in MRY with the restated number — so a backtest that forms a 2009 portfolio is using information from 2011. The strategy will look better than it was.

Use the as-reported dimensions, ARY and ARQ, for anything historical.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Filed, Not Ended


reportperiod
When the fiscal year ended. Nobody outside the company knew the numbers yet.


datekey
When it was filed with the SEC. This is the first day you could have acted on it.



Sorting on reportperiod gives you a few weeks to a few months of free information, every year, in every name. It is the single most common way a backtest in this course goes wrong.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Who Is in the Sample

Ask a question you cannot answer from the schema: does the data still contain companies that stopped existing?


If it holds only companies listed today, then every 2005 portfolio you form is made of firms you already know survived to 2026. That is not a small bias. It is the difference between a strategy and an illusion.

Tell GLM

Count distinct tickers with data in 2005. Then count how many of those still have data in the most recent year, and show me some that do not.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Three More







The peer median
Computed from the same date, or from data that arrived later?


Delisting returns
A company that goes to zero has to be recorded as going to zero


Costs and borrow
The short side is not free, especially in the small names




None of these will throw an error. Each of them makes the answer better than the truth.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Three Numbers


Average return
The mean of your annual long-short returns.


Standard deviation
How much those returns bounced around, year to year.


The ratio, and its t-stat
With twenty-five observations, the t-stat is doing a lot of work.



Twenty-five annual returns is a small sample. A strategy earning four percent a year with fifteen percent volatility is not distinguishable from nothing.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Compare It to Something

Four percent a year is a fact about your strategy. It is not yet a finding.



The market
Did the long side simply do what stocks did?


A random sort
Run it with the signal shuffled. What does noise earn in your backtest?


Value itself
Plain P/E, no peer group. Did the peer adjustment add anything?



The third comparison is the real test of last session’s work.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Look at the Years
Tell GLM

Plot the annual return of the long-short portfolio, year by year. Mark the best and worst years and tell me what the portfolio held in each.


An average built out of one enormous year and twenty-four small negative ones is a different animal from a steady four percent, and the summary statistics will not tell you which you have.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Three People, No Shared Memory

The conversation you had with GLM on Tuesday is invisible to your groupmates, and gone to you.


The code survives. The reasoning does not — why you used ARY, which peer definition you rejected, what you tried on the short side that did not work. That is exactly what the next person needs, and exactly what nobody writes down.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
What a Memory File Is


One file per session
Dated, in the repository, next to the code it describes.


Written by GLM
At the end of the session, from the conversation it just had. You correct it.


Read by GLM
At the start of the next session, before it touches anything.



It serves your groupmates and it serves the model. Both start every session knowing nothing.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
What Goes in It


Date, and who was working
What we set out to do
What we decided, and what we rejected — with the reason
What broke, and whether it is fixed
What is unfinished, and where to pick it up



Point 3 is the one that matters and the one that gets dropped. A decision without its reason gets re-litigated in two weeks.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Build the Skill
Tell GLM

Make a skill that writes a session memory file. It should trigger when I say we are wrapping up. Write to memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md with those five headings, drawn from this conversation. Keep it under a page.

Then a second one, or a line in CLAUDE.md:

At the start of every session, read the three most recent files in memory/.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Try It Now


Build the skill
Say: we are wrapping up
Read what it wrote — and fix what it got wrong about your own afternoon
Commit and push, so the other two can read it before Thursday



Step 3 is not optional. A memory file nobody checked is a confident record of a session that did not happen.

title: Trading on Predictions
text:
Three Things


Get the backtest running end to end, however crude
Re-run it with ARY and datekey, and record what changed
Write the memory file, and push it



Thursday we stop borrowing the peer median and start predicting the multiple — which turns valuation into a regression, and gives you something to compare today’s result against.

title: Getting Started
text:
One Folder, Not Your Workspace


The rule
The repository is a folder inside your workspace, named after your group.
All three of you end up with mgmt638-team1 sitting in your workspace.

Why it matters
Your workspace also holds things that are yours alone — data you pulled, an experiment that went nowhere. Those are not the group’s business.
And when everyone’s copy is at the same path, an instruction that works for one of you works for all of you.

title: Getting Started
text:
One Person Creates It
Tell GLM — one person in the group, once

Make a folder in my workspace called mgmt638-team1 and make it a git repository. Add a .gitignore for data/, *.parquet, *.duckdb, .env and __pycache__. Commit, then create a private GitHub repo of the same name and push to it.


Pick your own name. Everyone else in the group skips to the slide after next.

title: Getting Started
text:
Keep the Data Out

The .gitignore is not housekeeping. It is the difference between a repository that works and one that has to be rebuilt.


Twenty years of market data is a few hundred megabytes. GitHub refuses files over a hundred, and it refuses them after the upload — so the push fails, slowly, and now the history has to be surgically repaired.

Your code goes to GitHub. Your data gets pulled down again by running the code.

title: Getting Started
text:
When Git Pushes Back







What you see
What to say




rejected --- non-fast-forward
Someone pushed while you were working. “Pull their work, merge it with mine, then push.”


CONFLICT: automatic merge failed
You both edited the same lines. “Show me both versions, tell me which is which, and wait for me to choose.”




Two commands to refuse: git push --force and git reset --hard. Both clear the error message by throwing away work — often a groupmate’s. If GLM proposes either, say no and tell it to pull and merge instead.
